scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Pettathullal is a historic ritualistic tradition associated with the Sabarimala pilgrimage at Erumely in Kottayam district, Kerala.
The dance commemorates the joyful celebration of the local people following the mythological destruction of the demoness Mahishi by Lord Ayyappa.
Historically, the ritual involves two distinct communities: the Ambalappuzha group and the Alangadu group.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Pettathullal is celebrated annually on the 27th day of the Malayalam month of Dhanu during the Mandalam-Makaravilakku pilgrimage period (spanning November, December, and January).
The ritual signifies spiritual purification and the victory of good over evil as represented by Ayyappa's defeat of Mahishi.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is executed in group formations by pilgrims who chant "Ayyappa thinthakathom, Swamy thinthakathom" in rhythm with loud percussion ensembles.
Dancers leap and step rhythmically while holding wooden weapons such as sarakkol (arrows) and wooden maces.
First-time Sabarimala pilgrims (Kanni Ayyappas) carry a bundle filled with cereals and vegetables tied to a stick across their shoulders, alongside a mandatory wooden arrow.
Watch for Petta Thullal Step.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The ritual dance is accompanied by vibrant traditional instrumental ensembles, sacred mantras, and vocal hymns.
Key instruments specified in the traditional performance include Chenda melam (percussion ensemble), Nagaswaram (double-reed wind instrument), and Pambamelam (traditional drumming).
Listen for the Chenda, Nagaswaram, Pamba.

A powerful, resonant outdoor ritual sound environment dominated by the thunderous percussion of Chenda melam and Pambamelam, melodic lines from the Nagaswaram, and the collective vocal shouting and chanting of thousands of pilgrims.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Participants dress in tribal-style attire, smearing their faces and bodies with bright paints and charcoal.
They carry symbolic wooden weapons including sarakkol (arrows) and wooden maces.
Kanni Ayyappas also carry a shoulder stick with a tied bundle containing vegetables and grains.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The performance involves key traditional roles rather than individual artistic performers.

These include the Periyaswami (the chief elder/leader who receives Dakshina), the Kanni Ayyappas (first-time pilgrims who must perform specific rituals with wooden arrows), members of the Ambalappuzha and Alangadu traditional groups, and representatives of the Mahallu Jamaat committee of the Vavar mosque who welcome the dancers.
Two distinct traditional groups perform regional variations of the ritual on the same day: the Ambalappuzha group and the Alangadu group.

The ritual lineage is preserved through hereditary regional participation by the Ambalappuzha and Alangadu communities, passed down through generations of Sabarimala devotees and led by senior spiritual leaders known as Periyaswamis.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Pettathullal is a sacred pilgrimage ritual connected to Lord Ayyappa and the Sabarimala pilgrimage. Outsiders should respect all religious observances, dietary/fasting vows (vrata kalam), and local temple customs. Participation in the ritual steps and carrying of sacred items (such as the irumudikettu and sarakkol) is traditionally reserved for practicing devotees.

The physical setting spans three primary sacred sites in Erumely: beginning at the Petta Sree Dharmasastha temple (Kochambalam), passing around the adjacent Vavar mosque, and concluding at the Valiyambalam Sastha temple located 0.5 km away.
visual_brief.setting_notes: Pettathullal is celebrated annually on the 27th day of the Malayalam month of Dhanu during the Mandalam-Makaravilakku pilgrimage period (spanning November, December, and January). The ritual signifies spiritual purification and the victory of good over evil as represented by Ayyappa's defeat of Mahishi. It begins with 'Prayashchitham' (atonement for sins committed during the fasting period) through offerings of betel leaves and coins on the irumudikettu travel kit, followed by offering Dakshina (Pettapanam kettal) to the Periyaswami. The event also stands as a famous symbol of Hindu-Muslim communal harmony due to the integration of the Vavar mosque into the sacred procession.
